analysis.one_liner: Banned insured banks and credit unions from trading derivatives for their own profit.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee and never got a vote; it had one sponsor and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred federally insured banks from buying and selling derivatives — financial contracts whose value comes from interest rates, currencies, stocks, or bonds — for their own accounts, allowing them only to hedge their own risks and only tiny "de minimis" positions otherwise. Credit unions would have faced a flat derivatives ban. Bank holding companies could still trade derivatives through affiliates kept financially separate from the insured bank, as long as they told the public that those affiliate losses are not federally insured.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank depositors and, behind them, the federal deposit insurance fund and taxpayers. In the mid-1990s, insured banks had become major players in derivatives markets, and losses on those bets could land on the FDIC insurance fund — which is ultimately the taxpayer's backstop — if a bank failed. The bill would have moved that trading risk out of insured institutions while letting banks still hedge their own loans and holdings [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bank depositors, the FDIC fund, taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibited insured depository institutions and their affiliates from trading derivatives for their own accounts, with narrow exceptions for hedging and tiny positions, so deposit-insured money would no longer backstop speculative trading losses [S2][S3].

Required any separately capitalized affiliate still allowed to trade derivatives to clearly and publicly disclose that its assets and losses are not federally insured or guaranteed by the parent — protecting depositors from assuming that protection exists [S3].
Imposed an outright derivatives ban on insured credit unions and their affiliates [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large banks that earned substantial revenue from derivatives trading would have lost the ability to run those businesses inside insured banks; derivatives dealers would have lost insured-bank counterparties and trading volume. Credit unions would have lost any ability to use derivatives at all.

drawbacks.text: The core ban had a large built-in gap: a bank holding company's separately capitalized, non-bank subsidiaries could still trade derivatives for their own accounts, so much trading could simply move outside the insured bank rather than stop [S3].

The practical strength of the exceptions — what counts as hedging, what counts as a 'de minimis' interest — was left entirely to federal banking regulators to define through rules, so the bill's real effect would have depended on how strict those rules turned out to be [S2][S3].
The credit union provision was a blanket ban with no hedging or de minimis exception, going further than the bank provisions even though derivatives were a marginal business for credit unions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed at a real, taxpayer-relevant risk: losses on derivatives held by institutions whose deposits are federally insured. Its core ban on insured banks' own-account trading was well targeted. An honest supporter would acknowledge the design was porous — separately capitalized holding-company affiliates could keep the same trading alive outside the bank, and regulators would have had wide discretion in writing the hedging and de minimis exceptions. It was a meaningful but incomplete wall.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee in March 1995 and the committee never acted on it; it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. Byron Dorgan introduced the Derivatives Limitations Act of 1995 on March 15, 1995, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee [S1][S5].
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee held no hearing or markup and the bill never reached the Senate floor; its action history ends with the committee referral, and the Congress expired on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and derivatives dealers, whose derivatives trading inside insured institutions continued under the existing, more permissive rules because no restriction was ever enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large Wall Street banks and derivatives dealers

for.name: Sen. Byron Dorgan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it; he was its only supporter in the Senate record

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee (Chair Alfonse D'Amato, R-NY)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in March 1995 and never took the bill up — no hearing, no markup, no report — so it never reached the floor

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.industry: Large money-center banks and derivatives dealers
industries.note: The bill would have ended derivatives trading for banks' own accounts inside federally insured institutions, cutting off a major profit line. The industry's interest in keeping that revenue sat against depositors' and taxpayers' interest in keeping trading risk out of insured banks.

industries.industry: Bank holding companies and their nonbank affiliates
industries.note: The bill carved out a permanent legal channel: holding-company subsidiaries, if separately capitalized from the insured bank, could keep trading derivatives for their own accounts, with public disclosure that those losses are not federally guaranteed. It preserved much of the derivatives business while imposing capital separation and disclosure duties.

The bill imposed a flat derivatives ban on insured credit unions and their affiliates, with none of the hedging exceptions banks got. Derivatives were a marginal activity for credit unions, so the practical loss was small and the provision mainly served depositor safety.
